The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 & 6 \\ -2 & 2 & -4 \\ 6 & -4 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & -4 & -1 \\ 6 & -4 & 12 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & -4 & -1 \\ 3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -4 & 12 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -4 & 12 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-6{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & -3\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-2{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second row, we have 

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a-4b+c=-2-4\cdot \left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)+0=4.
$$

$$

$$

The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between two points where $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula:

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{4}{3}{x}^{3/2},$ $a=0,$ and $b=2.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=2\sqrt{x}
$$

Substituting ${f}^{′}(x)=2\sqrt{x}$ to the formula for the arc length, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{1+[2\sqrt{x}]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{1+4x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate this integral using the substitution $u=1+4x.$ Then, $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.$

We also need to compute new limits:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 2 \\ u & 1 & 9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}]|}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}({9}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{27-1}{6} \\  & =\frac{13}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =10.$ So, we get 

$$

$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-6{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2} &=0 \\ -6{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
